name: Prohormones (1-Andro, 4-AD)

card.summary: Steroid precursors once sold as supplements; androstenedione was banned in the US in 2004 and studies found little muscle benefit.
card.note: Androstenedione is a controlled substance in the US since 2005 and banned by sports bodies.

quick.overview:
Prohormones are compounds that the body can convert into active hormones. In the 1990s, androstenedione (4-AD, called andro) was sold over the counter as a supplement for raising testosterone and building muscle, and gained fame through baseball players.

Studies found that a single large dose raised testosterone variably and that daily lower doses had no effect on strength, muscle size or body fat. The US classed it as an anabolic steroid in 2004.
quick.mechanism: Androstenedione is a precursor in the pathway to testosterone and estrogens. Oral doses may be converted to testosterone in some people, and estradiol also rose in studies.
quick.risks: The FDA banned its sale in 2004, and a 2004 US law added it to controlled-substance schedules, effective 2005. It is banned by the WADA, the Olympics and major sports leagues. Reported effects in women included masculinization and menstrual disturbance.

lead: Prohormones are precursor compounds converted in the body to active hormones. In bodybuilding supplement culture the term covers androstenedione (4-AD, or andro) and related compounds such as 1-androstenedione, which were sold over the counter as testosterone boosters before regulatory action.[1]

Androstenedione was introduced to the North American supplement market with credit given to Patrick Arnold, and was used widely in Major League Baseball during the 1990s, including by Mark McGwire.[1] The International Olympic Committee banned it in 1997.[1] The FDA banned its sale on April 11, 2004, and the Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004, effective January 20, 2005, classed androstenedione and other prohormones under the Controlled Substances Act.[1]
infobox: Controlled substance since 2005; sale banned by FDA 2004
Prohibited by WADA, IOC, MLB, NFL, NBA, NCAA

paras: Through the 1990s androstenedione was legal and sold as a dietary supplement. From 1996 to 2001 Barry McCaffrey, then director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy, concluded it could not be classified as an anabolic steroid because there was no proof it built muscle.[1] The IOC banned it in 1997, and the FDA banned sales in April 2004.[1] The Anabolic Steroid Control Act, introduced March 12, 2004, took effect in January 2005 and added prohormones to the controlled-substance list.[1]

A 2000 study in JAMA found that a single 300 mg oral dose raised serum testosterone in young men over eight hours, while a 100 mg dose had no significant effect, and estradiol rose at both doses with wide individual variation.[1] A 2006 review found daily doses of 50 or 100 mg had no effect on strength, muscle size or body fat, and a study using a larger dose with other supplements also showed no strength gain.[1]

A 2021 review cited by Wikipedia describes a study of 10 healthy women given a dose of 100 mg, with reported voice deepening, hirsutism, menstrual irregularities and abnormal bleeding, blood clots and metabolic disruption.[1]

Human studies of androstenedione include the 2000 JAMA study of testosterone response in young men and a 2006 review of strength and body composition outcomes, summarized above.[1] No studies of 1-androstenedione were found in the sources reviewed.

timeline.event: A JAMA study measures testosterone response to oral androstenedione in young men.[1]
The FDA bans sale on April 11; the Anabolic Steroid Control Act is introduced March 12.[1]
The Anabolic Steroid Control Act takes effect January 20.[1]

lore.intro: Prohormones are remembered in bodybuilding communities as legal pro-steroid supplements of the 2000s.

claims.claim: Andro raises testosterone and builds muscle
claims.believers: Users and sellers in the supplement era said it acted like a mild steroid.
claims.experts: A 2006 review found 50 to 100 mg daily had no effect on strength, muscle size or body fat; a 300 mg dose raised testosterone variably.[1]

claims.claim: Prohormones are a safe legal alternative to steroids
claims.believers: Supplement marketing positioned them as legal and mild.
claims.experts: The FDA banned androstenedione in 2004 and the US classed it as a controlled anabolic steroid; reported effects in women included masculinization.[1]
